title: Hearing
lead: The ear turns a pressure wave into the sensations of pitch, loudness and timbre, and each of these rests on a physical quantity of the sound. This section gives the range of frequencies the ear hears, relates pitch to frequency and loudness to both intensity and frequency through the equal-loudness curves and the phon, shows how hearing loss is measured on an audiogram, and follows the sound through the ear canal, the lever of the middle ear and the cochlea to the nerves.
objectives: Define hearing, pitch, loudness, timbre, note, tone, phon, ultrasound, and infrasound.
Compare loudness to frequency and intensity of a sound.
Identify structures of the inner ear and explain how they relate to sound perception.
summary_html:
• The range of audible frequencies is 20 to 20,000 Hz.
  • Those sounds above 20,000 Hz are ultrasound, whereas those below 20 Hz are infrasound.
  • The perception of frequency is pitch.
  • The perception of intensity is loudness.
  • Loudness has units of phons.
notes: The band photograph that heads the section is left out, and so are the eight problems the book leaves unkeyed: the speedometer spanning a factor of 10³, the 2002 Hz and 1999 Hz sounds, the television going from 70 to 73 dB, the levels needed for 40 phons at 60, 3000 and 8000 Hz, the loudness of four frequencies at 60.0, 110 and 20.0 dB, the woman needing an amplification of 5.0 × 10¹², the intensities at 60 phons for 60.0 and 10,000 Hz, and the child with a 60 dB loss near 5000 Hz.
exercise_notes: Bloom levels, concept tags, weights and hints are AI-generated. Answers come from the book’s answer key. The Check Your Understanding on whether ultrasound and infrasound are imperceptible to all hearing organisms is keyed by the book and set inline after the passage that gives the hearing ranges of dogs, bats, dolphins and elephants. The one conceptual question, on why a hearing test can read 0 dB at 250 Hz when Figure 17.35 shows no one hears that frequency below 20 dB, has no key and is an open item with an AI-written suggested approach, marked as such. Nine problems are keyed and kept; the closest frequencies to 500 Hz and the five thresholds read from Figure 17.34 are set as several parts, since the book keys several numbers. Eight problems have no keyed answer and are left out: the speedometer spanning 10³, 2002 Hz against 1999 Hz, the television from 70 to 73 dB, 40 phons at 60, 3000 and 8000 Hz, the loudness of four frequencies at three levels, the 5.0 × 10¹² amplification, 60 phons at 60.0 and 10,000 Hz, and the child’s 60 dB loss near 5000 Hz. The section prints no AP item, nothing is taken from another section and nothing is held for a later one. Numeric answers accept 2% tolerance; the answers read from the equal-loudness curves are the book’s own readings, which it says carry uncertainties of several decibels.

figures.original_caption: The relationship of loudness in phons to intensity level (in decibels) and intensity (in watts per meter squared) for persons with normal hearing. The curved lines are equal-loudness curves—all sounds on a given curve are perceived as equally loud. Phons and decibels are defined to be the same at 1000 Hz.

The shaded region represents frequencies and intensity levels found in normal conversational speech. The 0-phon line represents the normal hearing threshold, while those at 40 and 60 represent thresholds for people with 40- and 60-phon hearing losses, respectively.

Audiograms showing the threshold in intensity level versus frequency for three different individuals. Intensity level is measured relative to the normal threshold. The top left graph is that of a person with normal hearing. The graph to its right has a dip at 4000 Hz and is that of a child who suffered hearing loss due to a cap gun. The third graph is typical of presbycusis, the progressive loss of higher frequency hearing with age. Tests performed by bone conduction (brackets) can distinguish nerve damage from middle ear damage.

This schematic shows the middle ear’s system for converting sound pressure into force, increasing that force through a lever system, and applying the increased force to a small area of the cochlea, thereby creating a pressure about 40 times that in the original sound wave. A protective muscle reaction to intense sounds greatly reduces the mechanical advantage of the lever system.

exercises.prompt: Are ultrasound and infrasound imperceptible to all hearing organisms? Explain your answer.

answer.solution: No, the range of perceptible sound is based in the range of human hearing. Many other organisms perceive either infrasound or ultrasound.

exercises.prompt: Why can a hearing test show that your threshold of hearing is 0 dB at 250 Hz, when Figure 17.35 implies that no one can hear such a frequency at less than 20 dB?

answer.solution: The two graphs measure different things. Figure 17.35 plots the sound intensity level itself, referred to $\kIo = 10^{-12}\ \text{W/m}^2$, and on that scale the normal threshold at 250 Hz is indeed about 20 dB, because the ear is less sensitive there than at 1000 Hz. An audiogram measures the threshold relative to the normal threshold at each frequency, so that a person with normal hearing registers 0 dB at every frequency tested. A reading of 0 dB at 250 Hz on a hearing test therefore means that your threshold at 250 Hz is the normal one, about 20 dB above $\kIo$, and not that you hear a 250 Hz sound of intensity $\kIo$.

exercises.prompt: The factor of $10^{-12}$ in the range of intensities to which the ear can respond, from threshold to that causing damage after brief exposure, is truly remarkable. If you could measure distances over the same range with a single instrument and the smallest distance you could measure was 1 mm, what would the largest be?

answer.hint: The largest distance is $10^{12}$ times the smallest. Multiply 1 mm by $10^{12}$ and convert the result to kilometers.

exercises.prompt: What are the closest frequencies to 500 Hz that an average person can clearly distinguish as being different in frequency from 500 Hz? The sounds are not present simultaneously.

parts.hint: Two sounds can be told apart when their frequencies differ by 0.3% or more. Take 0.3% of 500 Hz and subtract it.
The same 0.3% of 500 Hz, added instead of subtracted.

exercises.prompt: If your radio is producing an average sound intensity level of 85 dB, what is the next lowest sound intensity level that is clearly less intense?

answer.hint: At a given frequency a difference of about 1 dB can be discerned, but a change of 3 dB is what is easily noticed. The question asks for the level that is clearly less intense.

exercises.prompt: Based on the graph in Figure 17.34, what is the threshold of hearing in decibels for frequencies of 60, 400, 1000, 4000, and 15,000 Hz? Note that many AC electrical appliances produce 60 Hz, music is commonly 400 Hz, a reference frequency is 1000 Hz, your maximum sensitivity is near 4000 Hz, and many older TVs produce a 15,750 Hz whine.

parts.hint: The threshold of hearing is the 0-phon curve. Follow it to 60 Hz and read the intensity level from the vertical axis.
At 1000 Hz phons and decibels are defined to be equal, so the 0-phon curve passes through 0 dB there.
The curves dip below 0 dB where the ear is most sensitive, so the threshold at 4000 Hz is negative.
The 0-phon curve rises steeply at the high-frequency end of the range.

exercises.prompt: What is the approximate sound intensity level in decibels of a 600-Hz tone if it has a loudness of 20 phons? If it has a loudness of 70 phons?

parts.hint: Follow the 20-phon curve in Figure 17.34 to 600 Hz and read the intensity level from the vertical axis.
The 70-phon curve is nearly flat between 400 and 1000 Hz, so at 600 Hz it lies close to the level it has at 1000 Hz, where phons and decibels agree.

exercises.prompt: Suppose a person has a 50-dB hearing loss at all frequencies. By how many factors of 10 will low-intensity sounds need to be amplified to seem normal to this person? Note that smaller amplification is appropriate for more intense sounds to avoid further hearing damage.

answer.hint: Every 10 dB of intensity level is a factor of 10 in intensity, so a level 50 dB higher is $10^{50/10}$ times as intense.

exercises.prompt: (a) What is the intensity in watts per meter squared of a just barely audible 200-Hz sound? (b) What is the intensity in watts per meter squared of a barely audible 4000-Hz sound?

parts.hint: Read the threshold at 200 Hz from the 0-phon curve, about 23 dB, and convert the level to an intensity with $\kIntens = \kIo 10^{\beta/10}$, where $\kIo = 10^{-12}\ \text{W/m}^2$.
The threshold at 4000 Hz is about −7 dB, below 0 dB, so the intensity is less than $\kIo$.

exercises.prompt: A person has a hearing threshold 10 dB above normal at 100 Hz and 50 dB above normal at 4000 Hz. How much more intense must a 100-Hz tone be than a 4000-Hz tone if they are both barely audible to this person?

answer.hint: Find each tone’s threshold for this person by adding the loss to the normal threshold read from the 0-phon curve of Figure 17.34, about 37 dB at 100 Hz and −7 dB at 4000 Hz. The difference in levels gives the ratio of intensities through $\beta_2 - \beta_1 = 10\log_{10}(\kItwo/\kIone)$.

exercises.prompt: What is the ratio of intensities of two sounds of identical frequency if the first is just barely discernible as louder to a person than the second?

answer.hint: At a given frequency a difference of about 1 dB can be discerned. A difference of 1 dB in level is a ratio of $10^{1/10}$ in intensity.
